name: Projection bias
aliases: Projection bias in predicting future utility
statement: People know which way their tastes will move and underestimate how far, so a choice made while cold, hungry or craving is tilted towards the state of the person making it.
meaning: The economic version of the idea is a claim about magnitudes rather than about feelings. Loewenstein, O'Donoghue and Rabin assume that people understand the direction in which their tastes will change and underestimate the size of the change. Their formal statement, which they call simple projection bias, writes predicted utility as a weighted average of true future utility and utility evaluated in the current state, with one parameter alpha between 0 and 1. At alpha = 0 the prediction is right. At alpha = 1 the person expects her future tastes to be identical to her present ones. The model says nothing about how tastes actually change. It takes any pattern of change, from adaptation to a medical condition to the swing between hunger and satiation, and predicts that a person will allow for too little of it. That is what makes it a parameter to be estimated rather than a mood to be induced, and it is why the evidence for it is field data on purchases rather than laboratory manipulations of visceral state. The applications in the paper are economic. Under habit formation the bias makes people consume too much early in life and save too little, and it makes durable goods bought in an unusual state look better than they will prove to be.

origin.who: George Loewenstein, Ted O'Donoghue and Matthew Rabin
origin.note: The paper reviews psychological evidence, defines simple projection bias as a linear combination of current and future utility, and works out the consequences for life-cycle consumption, addiction and durable-goods purchases. It contains no new data. Its authors note that one observed decision rarely identifies the bias, and suggest looking for field analogues of Read and van Leeuwen's hunger experiment or for dynamic inconsistency across repeated observations of the same person.

evidence: The 2003 paper assembles other people's results. Sackett and Torrance are quoted as finding that non-patients rate chronic dialysis at 0.39 on a scale where 0 is as bad as death and 1 is perfect health, while dialysis patients rate their own state at 0.56. Van Boven, Dunning and Loewenstein's mug study is quoted with an average selling price of $6.37 against an average buying price of $1.85. Sellers guessed buyers would pay $3.93 and buyers guessed sellers would charge $4.39, each estimate falling between the two real figures. Table I of the paper reproduces Read and van Leeuwen's snack choices for delivery a week later. Of office workers who were hungry and expected to be hungry, 78% chose the unhealthy snack. The other three cells gave 56% for satiated people expecting hunger, 42% for hungry people expecting satiation and 26% for satiated people expecting satiation. The first field test came from Conlin, O'Donoghue and Vogelsang, two of whom wrote the model. A US outdoor apparel and gear company gave them every order in weather-related categories from January 1995 to December 1999, over 12 million items. That was cut to 2,200,073 orders across gloves and mittens, winter boots, hats, sports equipment, parkas and coats, vests and jackets. Return rates ran from 6.6% for sports equipment to 22.2% for parkas and coats. A fall of 30°F in the temperature on the order date raised the probability of a return by 0.57 percentage points, which is a 3.95% rise in the return rate. By category the effect ran from 1.44 percentage points for vests to 0.27 for parkas and coats, and was significant in six of eight specifications. Fitting the model to the same data put alpha between 0.31 and 0.50 in every category the authors could estimate except vests. Predicted tastes sat roughly a third to a half of the way from true future tastes back towards current tastes. Acland and Levy took the bias to a gym. They paid 120 students and staff at the University of California, Berkeley to attend, keeping 54 treated and 57 control people after attrition, and elicited predictions of later attendance before and after the incentive month. Attendance after the incentive ended rose by 0.188 visits per week. Treated people revised their predictions down by 0.421 visits per week less than controls in weeks carrying no extra incentive, which the authors read as a failure to foresee the habit they had just formed.

replication.headline: Three independent teams found the same over-influence of current conditions in cars, cinema tickets and health insurance, and none of them could separate projection bias from salience.
replication.detail: Busse, Pope, Pope and Silva-Risso used more than forty million new and used vehicle transactions from a 20% sample of US new-car dealerships between 1 January 2001 and 31 December 2008. A week 20°F warmer than normal for that location raised the convertible share of sales by 0.22 percentage points on a base of 2.6%, a rise of 8.5%. A snowstorm of about 10 inches raised the four-wheel-drive share by about 2 percentage points over the next two to three weeks, about 6% on a base of 33.5%. A 20°F rise cut the share of black vehicles by 0.26 percentage points on a base of 12.6%. Warm weather had no effect on convertible sales where the average daily high was already above about 80°F. Buchheim and Kolaska studied advance tickets for a Munich outdoor cinema, where the ticket is valid for one night, the show runs whatever the weather, and free forecasts are on the website. Orders were 40 to 50% higher on a completely clear day than on a completely cloudy one, at every purchase horizon from one day to four weeks ahead. Buyers who ordered in fine weather were also more likely to let the ticket expire. Chang, Huang and Wang matched Chinese health-insurance orders to daily air pollution. A one standard deviation rise in pollution raised contracts sold that day by 7.2%, and a one standard deviation fall during the cost-free cancellation period, relative to the order-date level, raised the return probability by 4.0%. That last figure repeats the catalogue design in a different market and a different country. All three teams name salience as an explanation that fits their data as well as projection bias does. The car paper registers that caution in its own title: the working paper was called 'Projection Bias in the Car and Housing Markets', the published article 'The Psychological Effect of Weather on Car Purchases'.

study.cite: Busse, M. R., Pope, D. G., Pope, J. C., & Silva-Risso, J. (2015). The psychological effect of weather on car purchases. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(1), 371-414.

limits: No field study has separated projection bias from salience, and every team that has run one says so. Buchheim and Kolaska rule out a salience account of product attributes and then report that projection bias, extrapolative expectations and a reminder effect all remain consistent with their findings. Chang, Huang and Wang report the most support for projection bias and salience together. The evidence is also thinner inside the papers than the headline numbers suggest. Conlin and colleagues' second prediction, that returns should rise with the temperature on the day the return decision is made, held only for winter boots, and they attribute the weakness to not observing when that decision was taken. Their structural estimate of alpha was near zero for vests. It could not be obtained with standard errors at all for gloves and mittens or for sports equipment, and for hats and winter boots only after dropping every order placed between February and August. Busse and colleagues looked for the catalogue paper's return effect by tracking vehicles that reappear as trade-ins. Only 2.37% of vehicles reappear within a year, and the convertible result was significant in one of three columns. It gives 0.34 percentage points more early returns per 20°F against a base of 7.332%. Acland and Levy analysed 111 people, and the attendance gain they call habit had fallen to 0.047 visits per week and lost significance after the winter break. Laboratory work is small. De-Magistris and Gracia auctioned sheep-milk cheese to 98 consumers, nine of whom were dropped for not reporting hunger. Currently hungry bidders paid 11 cents more on average for cheese delivered later, and 12.5 cents more when delivery was scheduled for a hungry moment. No meta-analysis of projection bias and no direct repetition of the catalogue study were located. Searches covered Crossref, Semantic Scholar and general web searches for replication and preregistration terms; PsycINFO, EconLit and OpenAlex were not searched.
misreadings: The gym-membership literature is routinely filed under projection bias and mostly does not belong there. DellaVigna and Malmendier followed 7,752 health-club members. Those on a flat monthly fee above $70 attended 4.3 times a month, paying more than $17 a visit where a ten-visit pass cost $10 a visit. That paper explains the choice by overconfidence about future self-control or future efficiency. Projection bias appears in it once, as something that might reinforce the effect. The gym study that does test projection bias is Acland and Levy's, and it tests prediction of a habit rather than choice of a contract. The 3.95% from the catalogue paper is a proportional change in the return rate, not 3.95 percentage points; the absolute figure is 0.57 percentage points. Alpha of a third to a half is an estimate from one company's orders under one model of catalogue returns, not a general constant. The name also travels in two other senses that this entry is not about. In social psychology, projecting one's own view onto other people is the false consensus effect, and projecting a disowned trait onto them is psychological projection. The nearest neighbours are closer still and remain distinct. The hot-cold empathy gap is Loewenstein's earlier framework and is restricted to visceral states such as hunger, pain, craving and arousal, tested by inducing those states in a laboratory. Projection bias applies to any taste change, including slow adaptation to a chronic illness, and is measured as a parameter in market data. Affective forecasting errors run the other way, in a sense worth keeping straight. There the complaint is that people expect an event to move them more than it does. Projection bias says people expect their own preferences to move less than they do.
